sections.title: Regions and datacenters
points: A region is a set of datacenters deployed within a latency-defined perimeter and connected by a dedicated low-latency regional network.
A geography (such as North America) contains multiple regions, so it is not a single region.
Not every region is guaranteed to have multiple datacenters; zones group one or more datacenters.
Many resources require you to choose a region at deploy time; data transfer between regions is billed, not always free.

sections.title: Azure Government
points: Azure Government is a separate Azure cloud built for US government compliance and security requirements.
Eligible customers: US federal, state, local and tribal government entities, and US contractors/partners that serve them.
Non-US government entities and contractors (for example European or Canadian) are not eligible.
Azure Government is operated by Microsoft.

sections.title: Azure China
points: Azure in China is a distinct, separate instance of Azure, physically isolated from global Azure.
It is operated by 21Vianet, not by Microsoft.
It does not have feature parity with global Azure and is not limited to access from inside China.

sections.title: What availability zones are
points: Availability zones are physically separate groups of one or more datacenters within a single Azure region, each with independent power, cooling and networking.
They are not spread across regions or continents, and they do not replicate data to multiple regions.
Not every Azure region supports availability zones; supporting regions have at least three.
Zones work with many services and with both Windows and Linux VMs, not only Windows Server VMs.

sections.title: Failures that zones protect against
points: Availability zones protect against datacenter-level (zone) failures, including smaller failures such as a rack or server.
They do not protect against a full region outage; use multiple regions for that.
Zone-redundant resources, including managed disks, survive the loss of one zone.
Failure scope, smallest to largest: server, datacenter/zone, region.

sections.title: Surviving a single datacenter failure
points: Deploying VMs to two or more availability zones keeps services running if one datacenter fails.
Deploying VMs to two or more regions also survives a datacenter failure (and a region failure), at greater cost and complexity.
Resource groups are only a management container and give no physical separation.
A single scale set is not by itself zone-resilient unless it is configured to span zones.

sections.title: VM SLA of 99.99 percent
points: Two or more VM instances spread across two or more availability zones in the same region give a 99.99 percent VM SLA.
Minimum for that SLA: 2 virtual machines in 2 availability zones.
An availability set (same datacenter) gives a lower SLA than zones.

sections.title: Datacenters, zones, and regions
points: A datacenter is the physical facility; Azure groups datacenters into availability zones and regions.
A region holds datacenters within a latency-defined perimeter, joined by a low-latency network.
An availability zone is a logical grouping of one or more physically separate datacenters with independent power, cooling and networking.

sections.title: Resource group behavior
points: A resource group stores metadata about its resources; its resources can be in different regions.
Each resource exists in exactly one resource group, and resource groups cannot be nested.
Deleting a resource group deletes all resources in it.
Resources can communicate with resources in other resource groups.
Tags and permissions: permissions assigned on a group are inherited by its resources; tags are not inherited automatically.

sections.title: Where resources are placed
points: Every Azure resource, such as a VM, is deployed into a resource group within a subscription.
A storage account is a resource itself, not a container for VMs.

sections.title: Subscriptions, tenants, and administrators
points: A subscription trusts exactly one Microsoft Entra tenant; a tenant can have many subscriptions.
You can change the directory associated with a subscription.
If a subscription expires, the Entra tenant is not deleted.
Subscriptions are managed with Entra accounts, not only Microsoft accounts; a subscription has one account administrator.
Separate Entra directories per division create more admin overhead than subscriptions.

sections.title: Multiple subscriptions and moving resources
points: One account can manage multiple subscriptions, and a company can use resources from many.
Subscriptions cannot be merged; instead move resources between subscriptions.
VMs and their associated resources can be moved to a different subscription.

sections.title: Subscription as billing and limit boundary
points: Create a subscription first as the container for billing and resources when starting in Azure.
Costs are billed per subscription, so give each department its own subscription to use different payment options.
Subscription quotas/limits are raised by creating a new support request (quota increase).

sections.title: Free trial and ownership
points: After a free trial expires you cannot start VMs; convert to pay-as-you-go to continue.
The Owner role manages resources but does not transfer the subscription; billing account administrators do.
A spending limit on a trial is fixed.

sections.title: Management groups
points: Management groups sit above subscriptions and let you apply governance, such as Azure Policy and access control, across multiple subscriptions.
Resource groups organize resources inside one subscription and cannot span subscriptions.
Azure Policy defines rules; management groups define the scope where they apply.

sections.title: Scope hierarchy
points: Order, top to bottom: management group, subscription, resource group, resource (such as a VM).
Settings such as policy and access assigned at a higher scope are inherited below.

sections.title: Segmenting Azure by department
points: Use separate subscriptions and/or resource groups to segment resources for departments, each with its own administrator.
Multiple regions do not provide administrative segmentation.
Multiple Entra directories add administrative effort and are not the usual approach.

sections.title: Compare compute services
points: Virtual machines: IaaS; full OS control and OS-level virtualization.
Container Instances: run containers without managing VMs; portable app environment.
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) and Container Instances both manage containers.
App Service: PaaS to build, deploy and scale web apps.
Functions: serverless, event-triggered code. VM Scale Sets: groups of identical VMs.

sections.title: IoT services
points: IoT Hub: managed service for bidirectional communication between IoT devices and Azure; ingests data from millions of sensors.
IoT Central: fully managed SaaS to connect, monitor and manage IoT devices at scale.
Azure Sphere: secured MCU hardware, custom Linux OS and security service for IoT devices.
Data Lake Storage holds large volumes of ingested data.

sections.title: AI, analytics, and app services
points: Azure Machine Learning: build, test and deploy predictive analytics.
Azure Bot Service: conversational bots. Functions: serverless code.
Databricks: Apache Spark-based analytics. Application Insights: detects anomalies in web apps.
Cosmos DB is a database, not a predictive analytics tool.

sections.title: Azure DevTest Labs
points: DevTest Labs reduces administrative effort for creating and removing many Windows or Linux VMs repeatedly, with templates and policies.
It is not a compute type like VMs or scale sets; it is a lab-management service for dev/test VMs.

sections.title: Azure Virtual Desktop
points: Azure Virtual Desktop is a desktop and app virtualization service delivering cloud-hosted Windows from any location.
It supports both full desktops and published apps.
Session hosts are not limited to Windows 10; Windows 11 and Windows Server are also supported.
A host pool supports multi-session, so connections can exceed the number of session hosts.

sections.title: Scale sets and availability sets
points: VM Scale Sets: identically configured VMs that can scale in and out automatically.
Availability sets: group VMs into fault domains and update domains within a datacenter.
Availability zones are separate datacenters; load balancers distribute traffic.

sections.title: Azure Spot virtual machines
points: Spot VMs use unused Azure compute capacity at deep discounts; capacity can be reclaimed.
Reserved VM Instances are a committed-term discount, not unused-capacity pricing.

sections.title: Deploying many temporary VMs
points: Azure DevTest Labs minimizes effort to create and remove many VMs.
Microsoft Managed Desktop manages end-user desktops; it is not for deploying batches of VMs.
Scale sets scale identical VMs, not customized Windows and Linux mixes.

sections.title: VM dependencies
points: Every Azure VM needs a virtual network (its network interface connects to a subnet), plus a disk and compute.
A public IP address, service endpoint or Azure Firewall is optional.

sections.title: Content delivery network
points: A CDN caches content such as video at edge locations near users for best worldwide playback.
Application Gateway, ExpressRoute and Traffic Manager do not cache content at the edge.

sections.title: App Service plan tiers
points: Free and Shared run on shared VMs and cannot scale out.
Basic, Standard and Premium run on dedicated VMs; features such as custom domains, TLS/SSL, autoscale and slots depend on tier.
Needs such as multiple dedicated instances with load balancing, custom domain and SSL point to Standard over Free, Shared or Basic.
Costs: choose the lowest tier that meets all requirements.

sections.title: Virtual network basics
points: A virtual network provides isolation and segmentation; use separate VNets for separate network segments.
VNets in the same region are not connected by default; VNet names are unique within a resource group.
Address spaces can overlap in a subscription but must not overlap for peered VNets.
Peering can connect any two VNets, across regions or subscriptions.

sections.title: Network security groups
points: An NSG filters inbound and outbound traffic with allow/deny rules; it controls ports and connection types between VMs.
Associate an NSG with a subnet or a network interface, not with a virtual network.
Sources can be IP addresses/CIDR, service tags or application security groups.
Default rules allow VNet and outbound internet traffic and deny other inbound traffic, so NSGs do not block all traffic.
A local network gateway is not a traffic filter.

sections.title: Allowing internet access to a VM
points: Allow inbound HTTP/ports to a VM by modifying the NSG rules.
Traffic Manager is DNS-based load balancing and does not open ports.
DDoS protection does not allow ports either.

sections.title: Firewall and DDoS protection
points: Azure Firewall NAT (DNAT) rules let internet users reach a server in a virtual network; network and application rules filter traffic.
One Azure Firewall can centrally limit inbound traffic across virtual networks.
DDoS Protection defends against attacks and provides attack reports.

sections.title: Hybrid connectivity
points: Site-to-Site VPN: on-premises VPN device to an Azure VPN gateway over an encrypted tunnel on the internet.
Point-to-Site (P2S) VPN connects individual remote client computers to a VNet.
ExpressRoute: dedicated private connection that does not use the public internet; uses BGP, operates at layer 3; multiple circuits supported.
Connecting on-premises needs a virtual network gateway (in a gateway subnet) and a VNet; a local network gateway represents the on-premises VPN device.

sections.title: Azure DNS
points: Azure DNS hosts custom DNS domains and supports both public and private zones.
Azure VMs can register names in Azure DNS automatically.

sections.title: User-defined routes and appliances
points: A network virtual appliance is a VM that performs a network function such as a firewall.
User-defined routes can control traffic beyond a single VNet's subnets.
NSGs can contain multiple inbound and outbound rules.

sections.title: Tools for running Azure scripts
points: PowerShell scripts run from Windows, Linux or macOS with Azure PowerShell installed.
Azure CLI works on Linux/macOS/Windows; Cloud Shell runs in a browser from any OS.

sections.title: Keeping storage traffic off the internet
points: A service endpoint keeps traffic from a virtual network to an Azure service (such as Storage) on the Microsoft backbone network.
A private endpoint gives the service a private IP address in your VNet.
A public endpoint is reachable over the internet; NSGs and VPN Gateway do not make PaaS traffic private.

sections.title: Azure Storage services
points: Blob: very large unstructured objects like video. Files: network file shares (SMB) mapped as drives.
Queue: reliable messaging between applications. Table: key/attribute NoSQL store.
Disk storage: VM disks; unmanaged VM disks are stored in blob containers.
Only Blob supports the Archive access tier.

sections.title: Database and analytics services
points: Cosmos DB: globally distributed NoSQL, JSON documents, multi-region writes.
SQL Database: managed relational database. Synapse Analytics: MPP data warehouse.
HDInsight: managed Hadoop/Spark clusters. Data Lake: store large analytics data.
Machine Learning predicts; IoT Hub ingests device data; Functions runs serverless code.

sections.title: Tier minimum retention and cost
points: Hot: frequently accessed, highest storage cost, lowest access cost.
Cool: infrequent, at least 30 days. Cold: at least 90 days. Archive: at least 180 days, lowest storage cost.
Deleting or moving data before the minimum period triggers an early deletion fee.

sections.title: Archive rehydration
points: Archive is offline: blobs can't be read until rehydrated to hot, cool or cold; this can take hours.
Archive can't be the default account tier.
Archive is supported only for LRS, GRS and RA-GRS accounts.

sections.title: Setting access tiers
points: The account default tier is hot or cool (or cold), and blob tiers can be changed after upload.
Archive is set per blob, not at account level.
Cool and archive are not recommended for active data; archive suits long-term backups.
Tiering applies to block blobs, not premium storage.

sections.title: Number of copies
points: LRS keeps 3 copies in one datacenter.
ZRS 3 copies across zones; GRS 6 copies (3 + 3 in secondary region); GZRS 6 copies.
Storage always keeps at least three copies, but LRS isn't backed up to another datacenter.

sections.title: Read access to the secondary region
points: GRS does not allow reads from the secondary; RA-GRS does.
Choose RA-GRS or RA-GZRS for data on multiple nodes in separate regions with reads from both.

sections.title: Ordering redundancy options
points: Least to most redundant: LRS, ZRS, GRS (GZRS highest).
LRS protects drive/rack failures; ZRS adds zone failures; GRS adds region failures.

sections.title: Premium block blob redundancy
points: Premium block blob accounts support LRS and ZRS only, not geo-redundancy.
GRS, GZRS and their read-access variants are available for standard general-purpose v2 accounts.

sections.title: Premium account types
points: Premium performance accounts include block blobs and file shares (and page blobs).
Standard general-purpose v2 is the standard account type, not a premium type.
Premium accounts use SSD storage for low latency.

sections.title: Creating storage accounts
points: Create an Azure file share inside a storage account.
Storage account names must be globally unique across Azure, regardless of region or subscription.

sections.title: File transfer and sync tools
points: AzCopy: command-line utility to copy blobs or files to or from a storage account.
Azure Storage Explorer: graphical app for managing storage, not a migration service.
Azure File Sync: syncs Windows Server files with an Azure Files file share.

sections.title: Data Box and Azure Migrate
points: Azure Data Box is a physical device to move large amounts of data quickly and inexpensively.
Azure Migrate discovers, assesses and migrates on-premises servers and workloads.
Azure File Sync syncs files and Databricks is an analytics service.
